Gulf countries said on Wednesday, November 18, they intercepted missiles and drones from Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, after the United States struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking an uptick in hostilities despite efforts to end the nine-month-old war.

The back-and-forth attacks were a reminder of the hurdles facing diplomatic efforts to end a war that has destabilized the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and helped fuel the US voter anger that punished President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the November elections.

The Iranian army said it had targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base, after the US ally said its air defenses were countering hostile drone attacks. It was the first Iranian attack on the oil-rich country since September.

blocks.caption: Iran, Oman foreign ministers discuss safeguarding maritime corridors

blocks.text: Neighboring Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks for the third time this week. It accused Tehran of maintaining a “systematic hostile approach” of targeting the country, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen said it destroyed a cruise missile launched by the militia toward the Saudi capital of Riyadh.

On Tuesday, November 17, on the opposite side of the Gulf, US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island, said a US military official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The official said the strike was in response to Iran’s attacks on US personnel and assets.
Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure.

Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack on Washington, when asked about a CNN report that cited US intelligence assessments on a potential Iranian plot involving a so-called dirty bomb.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry had denied the allegations on Tuesday, calling them “baseless.”

A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to disperse radioactive material. Unlike a nuclear weapon, it does not produce a nuclear explosion, but can spread radioactive contamination and cause significant disruption and public alarm.

There are diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict, which started when the US and Israel struck Iran on February 28 and has since widened to include Iranian strikes on Israel and US assets in the Middle East.
Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at “bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground,” Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.

That followed a visit to Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, where he held talks on safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, Oman’s Foreign Ministry said.
Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global energy supplies before the war but which is now partly blocked by Iran.
Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he met Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran’s diplomatic initiative to end the war.
Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
A surge in tanker attacks since October threatens to further strain global oil supplies. On Tuesday, a crew abandoned a liquefied petroleum gas tanker off Oman’s Khasab.

Meanwhile, Iran has kept pressure on Washington through its Houthi allies, who have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia — the world’s largest oil exporter — while tightening control over Yemen’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opposite Hormuz, in an effort to squeeze Gulf oil producers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Burnham considering cuts to national insurance to create more youth jobs
articles.summary: PM hints he is open to suggestion in Milburn report to lower NICs contributions paid by companies for under-25s

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”.
The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government.

On Tuesday, a report suggested national insurance contributions (NICs) paid by firms for under-25s should be gradually lowered, starting with retail and hospitality companies, to help create more jobs.
The independent report, by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, also proposed doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

Asked if he believes the last government was wrong to increase NICs, Burnham told LBC: “I think it’s something you’ve got to consider very carefully going forward. Obviously, I’ve come in [and] inherited the situation.
“I think the last government was right to offer support to employers to take on young people. So, that was one of the things that they did through the Youth Guarantee.

“I will want to look at all of the evidence in relation to it, but also the affordability of making any change to national insurance. There is an exemption for young people up to 21, so there is some [movement] that’s been done in that area.
“But I can’t give you a firm commitment today because obviously these matters are matters for the budget more broadly.”

Currently, businesses do not pay employer NICs for workers younger than 21 nor for apprentices under 25 unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. For non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. Official figures show there are nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK.

On the backbench rebellion to the last proposed reforms to welfare, Burnham told LBC: “Well, it is a very different proposition. First and foremost, it’s about support for young people, opportunity for young people.
after newsletter promotion

“It’s not about an arbitrary number for cuts within the system. You’ve got Conservatives and Reform who are going that way. It’s the crude cuts approach, and it just doesn’t work. It’s why they left office with a million Neets, and we’re going to have to do something fundamentally different.

“I think Alan Milburn has laid out what that looks like. It is also about a very different way of providing support, so not the old top-down tick-box system of the past, but a much more localised approach.”

articles.title: Body found in Derry bog decapitated more than 2,000 years ago, coroner finds
articles.summary:
Inquest-style inquiry concludes iron age remains are of 15- to 22-year-old female who may have been ritually sacrificed

A coroner’s investigation into

blocks.text: A coroner’s investigation into Northern Ireland’s most venerable cold case has concluded that the victim was decapitated more than 2,000 years ago.

The inquest-style inquiry determined that Ballymacombs More Woman – the name given to iron age remains found in a County Derry bog three years ago – was between 15 and 22 years old when she was beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.

The inquiry, hosted at the Ulster Museum on Monday, was not a formal inquest but adopted the structure and methodology of a coroner’s investigation and drew on the latest archaeological, forensic and scientific evidence to examine the death.

blocks.caption: Jen Gosman and Niamh Baker of National Museums NI examine a woven artefact found with Ballymacombs More Woman. Photograph: Kelvin Boyes Press Eye/National Museums NI

blocks.text: “The purpose of the exercise is not to impose modern legal conclusions upon the distant past, but to provide a framework through which the available evidence could be assessed and the story of a previously unknown young woman could be told,” said the coroner for Northern Ireland, Joe McCrisken, who chaired the investigation.

“Although separated from us by more than 20 centuries, she was once a living member of her community, and the investigation sought to restore, insofar as possible, an understanding of her life, death and place in history.”

The precise circumstances surrounding the woman’s death remain unknown, but evidence suggests it was part of a tradition of ritualised killing and sacrifice documented among other iron age bodies discovered across north-western Europe.

“What we have learned from this detailed research has allowed us to share her story with clarity and confidence,” said Hannah Crowdy, the head of curatorial at National Museums NI. “She has provided a significant insight into the iron age, and how we as a society have evolved over time.”

Peat workers discovered the remains in a bog in the townland of Ballymacombs More outside Bellaghy in October 2023, leading to an archaeological excavation which uncovered bones – though no skull – and a woven artefact.

blocks.caption: The woven artefact found alongside Ballymacombs More Woman. Photograph: Kelvin Boyes Press Eye/National Museums NI

blocks.text: Initially thought to be male, the body was called Bellaghy Boy until it was found to be female and renamed Ballymacombs More Woman. Residents in the area have given her a different name: Áine, after a mythical goddess.

Previous bog body discoveries such as Ireland’s Clonycavan Man and Denmark’s Tollund Man and Grauballe Man have given researchers insights into iron age societies. They also inspired poetry by the late Nobel laureate, Seamus Heaney, who grew up near Bellaghy.
after newsletter promotion

The coroner’s investigation had the imprimatur of the lady chief justice, Siobhan Keegan, as part of the judiciary’s outreach programme. It drew on specialists from Irish, UK and Danish universities and interviewed witnesses including Police Service of Northern Ireland officers and employees of Bulrush Horticulture, whose work led to the discovery of the remains.

blocks.caption: Hannah Crowdy of National Museums NI and the coroner Joe McCrisken (centre) with partners involved in the research process. Photograph: Kelvin Boyes Press Eye/National Museums NI

blocks.text: Using techniques such as micro-CT scanning, digital mapping and 3D imaging, the inquiry strove to establish who the deceased was and where, when and how she died.

The remains provided a bridge to the iron age, said Crowdy. “Her legacy will provide a crucial resource for research and learning, and an important reminder of how relevant museums are in connecting the past to the present day, not only for our visitors, but across academia too.”

articles.title: ‘I didn’t notice his body being purple’: Byron Bay doula left newborn to inflate a jumping castle, court hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into deaths of four babies born in free births or at home in northern NSW between 2022 and 2024 hears ‘something was seriously wrong’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Baby DH was born in an inflatable pool, in a candle-lit room in his parents’ home near Byron Bay, with no one medically trained present. There are two very different versions of what happened next.

In the parents’ version, the doula reassured them Baby DH was OK, then left to inflate a jumping castle while their newborn turned purple, became floppy, and struggled to breathe. In the doula’s version, everything seemed OK but she suggested they seek more help if they wanted to.
The New South Wales coroner’s court heard the two competing narratives on Wednesday as part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births.
The babies died in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
Baby DH lived for just over eight hours.
“The evidence will be that from his first minutes of life, [Baby DH] showed signs that something was seriously wrong,” the Lismore courtroom heard.
“His parents saw those signs. They raised them again and again with their doula, who they had engaged to watch for exactly that. Their doula, in this case, was a woman named Amy Lou Smith.
“Each time the parents raised their concerns, they were reassured by Amy Lou. An ambulance was not called until moments before [Baby DH] stopped breathing.”

His father described the baby as floppy after birth. “His colour, his whole body was purple with his hands and feet darker still,” the court heard, and Smith told them some purple in the hands and feet was normal.
“I didn’t notice his body being purple,” Smith told the court.

Told the baby’s colour wasn’t improving, Smith said “as long as his abdomen isn’t purple”, according to evidence from the parents. The mother was shocked. His whole body had been purple all along. His temperature was low, 34.5C. Smith suggested trying to get it up to 37C.
“I believed if they had real concerns, that they would call an ambulance and not be texting a non medically trained doula,” Smith told the court.
Smith, the inquest heard, described his laboured breathing as “cute little noises”. “I didn’t say that,” Smith told the court.
The court heard Smith told the couple Baby DH would have been put on oxygen if he was in hospital. But Smith later told the court she didn’t know what the hospital would have done.

He had strange lumps on his body, and wasn’t feeding. Smith suggested they get the lumps checked out, and warned that babies sometimes take a while to latch on to the breast, according to the parents’ evidence.
The court heard Smith left to set up a jumping castle for her son’s birthday. She sent the couple a picture of the castle later, as they were trying to contact a doctor, the court heard.
Smith told the court the castle was already set up, and the couple was happy for her to leave.
“Everything felt like it was OK,” she said.

Eventually, the parents spoke to the GP they had tried to contact earlier. The GP told them to call triple zero. They did, and did CPR until the paramedics got there. But Baby DH was declared dead at the hospital.
After the father had made the emergency call, Smith also told them to call an ambulance, and sent them instructions on infant CPR.
Throughout the hearing, Smith denied that any of her advice or comments constituted clinical advice.

Neonatologist Dr Paul Evans, the court heard, had found Baby DH had a complex heart defect, one that would have shown up on an X-ray. The baby could have been treated, and a birth plan with proximity to a major hospital and specialist cardiac care prepared, the court heard.
The child’s death was not inevitable, Evans found.

While pregnant, Baby DH’s mother decided to rely on a doula. She first approached a woman the court heard was likely to be Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper who was also involved in the care of another baby previously mentioned during the inquest. But Kali didn’t feel she could help, so they turned to Smith.
The court heard the couple paid for an online “sovereign birth course” for Smith and was reassured that she had enough experience. They agreed on an emergency plan.
Smith, who became a birth doula in 2020, was quizzed on her experience in court.
She has a degree in fine art and has worked as a social worker and a youth worker.

She told the court she is not medically trained in any way but did an online “full-spectrum doula course”. She learned CPR but was not familiar with how to apply it to a newborn – she denied she had given the parents the impression she was.
She had no training about a newborn’s colour, breathing, or feeding, but she did go to a retreat where she learned about referring a woman to more support if needed.

She had been present at 15 births over four years, nine alongside a midwife, and conceded she didn’t know what a low-risk birth would look like. She had read a couple of books about birthing, but they were more “spiritual”, the court heard.
She agreed that she now believes the best model of care for a home birth is for a clinically trained midwife to work alongside a doula.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Donald Trump calls Venezuela a US 'new acquisition'
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday described Venezuela as the country's "new acquisition," drawing attention to Washington's control over the South American nation's energy resources.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 3:46pm
United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday described Venezuela as the country's "new acquisition," drawing attention to Washington's control over the South American nation's energy resources.
"Venezuela, which was our new acquisition," Trump said during a speech ahead of his bilateral talks with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang.
"It was an acquisition, whether people like to say that or not. And it's been amazing what's happened to the United States," he added.
Trump made the remarks while discussing the United States' energy supply, making the country supposedly the world's leading producer of oil and natural gas "by a lot."
"We have more energy than any country in the world by double, even more than that. If you add Russia and Saudi Arabia together, we're much bigger than those two combined," he said.
"And then you add Venezuela, which was our new acquisition. It was an acquisition whether people like to say that or not. And it's been amazing what happened to the United States," Trump added.

Trump said the United States was looking to expand its energy exports to allies in the Pacific, including the Philippines, citing a planned major pipeline project in Alaska and the country's vast oil and natural gas reserves.
In January, US forces attacked Venezuela and ousted its longtime President, Nicolás Maduro.
Following what he described as a "successful" overnight military operation, Trump said US forces would remain in Venezuela until a new government was established.

Venezuela has millions of barrels of oil loaded on tankers and stored in storage facilities that it has been unable to ship because of a US blockade on its oil exports imposed by Trump in mid-December 2025.
The blockade was part of Washington's escalating pressure campaign against the Maduro government.
Trump arrived at Malacañang on Wednesday for his state visit to the Philippines.
During his meeting with Marcos, Trump announced that the two countries had secured a "big" trade deal but did not provide further details.
Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez, meanwhile, said the agreement involved food and energy supplies.
"The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements," he said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday afternoon left Manila to participate in the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders" Meeting in Shenzhen, China.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 3:27pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Wednesday afternoon left Manila to participate in the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China.
The PR001 carrying the President and his delegation left Villamor Air Base at 3: p.m.

With Marcos are First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, Finance Secretary Frederick Go, Trade and Industry Secretary Cristina Roque, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, and Presidential Communications Office Secretary Lino Cayetano.
They are expected to land at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport past 5 p.m.

articles.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% as energy prices increase
articles.summary:
October annual rate piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy

Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October amid an increase in energy prices…

blocks.text: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October amid an increase in energy prices triggered by the war in the Middle East.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September. City economists had forecast a reading of 3.6%.

As households brace for the colder winter months, the latest figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October. Driven by rising wholesale gas prices, forecasters are warning of a further increase of as much as a quarter from January.

Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide.
At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20 million households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm.
However, forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war.
Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year.

articles.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
articles.summary: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.

blocks.text: Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.
After legal challenges, state courts ruled the second Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.
Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration then filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could simply choose each man as their first and second choice.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would re-allocate any votes from the non-incumbent Dan Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to the US Senator.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for the other Dan Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Peltola would still have won.

The seat initially was one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the Senate - but by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50%, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

articles.title: Trump says US, Philippines sealed ‘biggest’ trade deal
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump said on Wednesday, November 18, the US had concluded a major trade agreement with the Philippines.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 2:50pm
US President Donald Trump (L) and Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr attend a luncheon at Malacanang Palace in Manila on Nov. 18, 2026.
AFP / Mandel Ngan
MANILA, Philippines — United States President Donald Trump said on Wednesday, November 18, the US had concluded a major trade agreement with the Philippines.

“We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far. And it’s a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said at a state luncheon hosted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang Palace. He said the deal had not been expected but “took place very quickly.”
No further details have been given as of posting.

Marcos and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton confirmed at the start of the bilateral talks today that a deal under Pax Silica, the US-led supply-chain initiative on critical technologies and minerals, would not be signed during Trump's visit.

Tariff situation. Philippine exports have faced an additional 12.5% US tariff since July 24, imposed after Washington said it found the Philippines had not adopted and effectively enforced a ban on imports made with forced labor.
This specific duty replaced a 10% levy imposed after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s earlier reciprocal tariffs. Under those reciprocal tariffs, Manila had been given a 19% rate.
In August, Malacañang said the government was negotiating to bring the rate down to 10%, which is the rate the US charges countries that have adopted or committed to forced-labor import bans.
Trade Secretary Cristina Roque earlier confirmed Manila would raise the topic of tariffs in Wednesday’s talks and disclose the outcome afterward.

Earlier, at the bilateral meeting, Trump said Manila and Washington were “going to probably do something very big” on nuclear energy. He also offered US gas from a planned Alaska pipeline to supply the Philippines.

articles.title: Speaker calls on ASEAN lawmakers to pass laws to increase trade among members, address AI dangers
articles.summary: Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Wednesday called on Southeast Asian lawmakers to pass laws which will increase trade and other avenues of cooperation in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations…

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 2:32pm

Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III on Wednesday called on Southeast Asian lawmakers to pass laws which will increase trade and other avenues of cooperation in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), saying goods should freely flow in the 11-strong regional bloc.
Dy made the call during his keynote speech during the opening of the 47th General Assembly of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly.

“Prosperity for all is the very purpose of ASEAN. And parliaments hold the tools to deliver it: laws that open markets fairly, budgets that build roads, ports, and schools, and oversight that ensures the benefits reach those who need them most,” Dy said.

“Growth should widen the circle. A rice farmer should receive a fair price for her harvest. A fisherman should be able to sell his catch in other towns. A small business in a provincial market should be able to reach customers in ten other countries. And a young graduate should be able to find work that makes full use of her talent,” Dy added.
Likewise, Dy said ASEAN lawmakers should stand together in fighting the challenges of artificial intelligence (AI) and regulating its benefits.

“Our farmers are already experiencing the digital transformation. Today, a farmer in the Mekong Delta checks the weather and the price of rice on her phone before deciding when to harvest. A young developer in Laos writes code for a company in Malaysia. A weaver in the Philippines sells her fabric to buyers in Indonesia. This is the ASEAN of 2045 arriving ahead of time. But the same networks also carry scams, disinformation, and threats to our privacy,” Dy said.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone. Our parliaments must therefore learn from one another and move forward together: on cybersecurity, consumer protection, the responsible use of AI, and extending connectivity to the last village still waiting for it,” Dy added.

Ultimately, Dy said working together shared prosperity is anchored on the ASEAN’s Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia inked 50 years ago, a commitment that is much needed today as the ASEAN countries bear the brunt of high oil prices amid the war between the United States and Iran.

“Their promise was simple and brave: we will respect one another, we will settle our differences peacefully, and we will work together. Half a century later, that promise still holds. That commitment matters more than ever,” Dy said.

“This year, conflict far from our shores led to higher fuel prices, and families in every one of our countries felt the impact. Through every challenge, the spirit of the Treaty has been our anchor. As parliamentarians, we are the guardians. We keep it alive every time we pick up the phone to reach a counterpart across the border, every time we disagree in this hall and yet part as friends,” Dy added. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
articles.summary: The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.

image.caption: The so-called 'blue tsunami' that saw Democrats sweep to victory across the US has swept across AlaskaImage: Lindsey Wasson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.
Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.
The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.
Peltola promises to deliver for 'Alaska's working families'
"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.
Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.
Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.
Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress
Vote siphon allegations

The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.
The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.
The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.
"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.
Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.

The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

articles.title: ‘Zero’ evidence that recent cascade of tech outages are linked, says Rubio
articles.summary:
The US secretary of state was speaking after Microsoft, major banks, and the National Security Agency were all affected by technical failures in recent days

US secretary of state Marco Rubio…

blocks.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the cascade of service outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or to a malign actor.

In recent days, Microsoft, major US banks, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Donald Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike demand the White House answer for the disruptions.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

He made the comments as he travelled with Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.

Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila.

The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, paralysing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”.
Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.

By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JP Morgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related”.
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.

“What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. Later, she praised the White House for having director of national intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.

“Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber-attack incident,” Clayton said, explaining that the US government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.

Democrat Mark Warner, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee reiterated that message, saying “there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.

“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change.
“The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

The post’s caption said:
"THE PEOPLE REMEMBER. HISTORY DOESN'T LIE. AND NO AMOUNT OF PROPAGANDA CAN CHANGE THAT." ???? Strong, direct, and unapologetic. #DUTERTELEGACY #PROUDFILIPINO
Rating: This is false.
Facts
Every clip included in the post was taken from the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony, misrepresented as footage from the 2017 ASEAN Summit hosted by the Philippines under Duterte.
The Threads post’s compilation of clips was taken from a 2024 TikTok reel posted by a pro-Duterte account praising the former president's leadership.
The SEAG Network uploaded footage of the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony at the Philippine Arena on November 30, 2019.
The footage used was sourced from the opening ceremony of the 2019 SEA Games held at the Philippine Arena, uploaded by the SEAG Network on YouTube on November 30, 2019.
The Duterte administration allocated P15.5 billion for the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN summit and related activities in 2017, not P7 billion as claimed in the video.
In comparison, the Marcos administration allocated a P22.9-billion budget for the 2026 ASEAN Summit hosted by the country.
Why we fact-checked this
The Philippines turned over the ASEAN chairship to Singapore on November 17, the final day of the bloc's 49th Summit.
Criticism over the P22.9-billion allocation for the 2026 ASEAN chairship prompted Malacañang to clarify that the amount also covers the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May 2026.
Preparations for the November summit included major infrastructure and venue preparations at the Philippine International Convention Center and World Trade Center in Pasay City.
As of November 18, the Threads post has garnered more than 2,000 likes and 100 reposts.

articles.title: Palace: Keeping streets clean post-ASEAN not government's job alone
articles.summary: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro urged Filipinos to practice proper trash disposal and help maintain cleanliness after the regional gathering.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:35pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. hands over the ceremonial wooden gavel to Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, marking the transfer of the ASEAN chairmanship on November 17, 2026.
The STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos must also do their part to keep the streets clean after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in an interview with DZRH on Wednesday, November 18.

"Madalas naman nagki-clearing din ang Metropolitan Manila Development Authority, 'di ba? Kaya lang syempre 'pag nag-clearing ka, may magtatakbuhang mga illegal vendors. 'Pag may nangyari, ikaw na naman ang sisisihin. Ang paglilinis ng Pilipinas ay hindi lang sa gobyerno," Castro said.

(The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority often conducts clearing operations, doesn't it? But when you conduct clearing operations, some illegal vendors run away. If something happens, you get blamed again. Keeping the Philippines clean is not solely the government's responsibility.)
Her remarks came after cleanup and clearing operations for the 49th ASEAN Summit drew criticism, including allegations that the government was attempting to conceal poverty from visiting delegates.
Large fences and barriers featuring artworks by Filipino National Artists were installed along key motorcade routes in Pasay City.
Rep. Antonio Tinio (ACT Teachers party-list) alleged that the barriers were intended to hide poor communities from visiting delegates.
Some street vendors along these routes were also ordered to temporarily close their stalls for the duration of the summit.

The preparations have also drawn scrutiny over the P22.9 billion allocated for the Philippines' ASEAN hosting activities in 2026. Malacañang previously said the amount covers the country's yearlong chairmanship and related events, not just the November summit.
Castro reiterated the importance of personal responsibility in keeping the country clean, particularly through proper trash disposal.
"Sabi nila, 'Kaya niyo na mag-abroad pero 'yong magtapon ng basura sa tamang basurahan, hindi niyo magawa ... Dito lang napakadaming reklamo.'"
(They say, "You can afford to travel abroad, but you can't even throw your trash in the proper bin ... There are just so many complaints here.")
The 49th ASEAN Summit officially concluded on Tuesday, November 17, with the Philippines formally handing over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore for 2027.
Related engagements, including US President Donald Trump's visit, continued on November 18.

articles.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
articles.summary: The Lobito Corridor is at the centre of a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals.

blocks.text: As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.

It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.

Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."

DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.

A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.

The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.

The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.

When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.

"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.

The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.

"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."

At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support ⁠local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

articles.title: Who is Timor-Leste's dancing prime minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão?
articles.summary: Xanana Gusmão's dancing drew cheers at ASEAN, but his political career stretches back to Timor-Leste's decades-long struggle for independence.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:08pm

MANILA, Philippines — He danced with Filipino performers to the beat of P-pop group SB19, drew cheers from fellow Southeast Asian leaders and became one of the crowd favorites at the closing ceremony of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila.
The man was Timor-Leste Prime Minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão, who joined performers dancing to SB19's rendition of "Together in Motion," the official theme song of the 2026 ASEAN Summit.
But it was not the first time he danced during his visit. He also joined in when Filipino young artists welcomed him upon his arrival and showed off a few moves during the summit's opening night.

But Gusmão is known for more than his dancing. Before becoming prime minister, he led the armed resistance against Indonesia's occupation of East Timor, spent years in prison and later became the country's first president after independence.
From journalist to resistance leader
Born on June 20, 1946, in Manatuto, Gusmão grew up when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule, according to the Timor-Leste government's official biography.
He worked in public administration before joining the Portuguese military. He later became a journalist and photographer for the newspaper A Voz de Timor.

His involvement in the independence movement began in 1974, when he joined the Timorese Social Democratic Association, which later became the Revolutionary Front for an Independent East Timor, or FRETILIN.

Indonesia invaded East Timor on Dec. 7, 1975, shortly after the territory declared independence from Portugal. The occupation led to years of armed resistance and a long struggle for self-determination.
Gusmão became one of the leading figures in that resistance. After the death of FRETILIN leader Nicolau Lobato in 1978, he helped reorganize the movement.
In 1981, he was elected leader of the resistance and commander-in-chief of its armed wing, the Armed Forces for the National Liberation of East Timor, or FALINTIL.
He also worked to unite different groups seeking independence. In 1988, he helped establish the National Council of Maubere Resistance, which later became the National Council of Timorese Resistance.
Imprisonment and independence
According to the Timor-Leste government's official biography, Indonesian forces captured Gusmão on Nov. 20, 1992, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

His arrest did not end his involvement in the independence movement. He continued to communicate with resistance leaders while in detention and used his time in prison to study Indonesian, English and law. He also wrote poetry and painted.
He was transferred to house arrest in February 1999 and released on September 7 that year.

Months earlier, on Aug. 30, 1999, East Timorese voted in a United Nations-backed referendum on whether to accept an autonomy proposal within Indonesia. A majority rejected the proposal, paving the way for the end of Indonesian rule.
Timor-Leste became an independent country on May 20, 2002, and Gusmão was elected its first president.
He served until 2007, when he became prime minister. He returned to the post in 2012 but resigned in 2015, saying he wanted to give younger leaders an opportunity to take over.

Gusmão remained involved in government, later serving as minister of planning and strategic investment. He also led negotiations with Australia over maritime boundaries, which resulted in a treaty ratified in 2019.
He returned as prime minister on July 1, 2023, after his party, the National Congress for Timorese Reconstruction, won the parliamentary elections.
Timor-Leste's decades-long bid to join ASEAN
Timor-Leste's push to join ASEAN began decades before it became the bloc's 11th member.

President José Ramos-Horta has been among the country's strongest advocates for regional integration. He discussed the idea with then-Indonesian Foreign Minister Adam Malik as early as 1974, when Timor-Leste was still under Portuguese rule.

Ramos-Horta, who served as president from 2007 to 2012 and returned to the post in 2022, also helped advance the country's bid for membership. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996 for his work toward a peaceful resolution of the conflict in East Timor.
Timor-Leste formally applied for ASEAN membership on March 4, 2011, during Ramos-Horta's presidency, with Gusmão then serving as prime minister.
The application, however, did not lead to immediate membership. ASEAN had to assess whether the young country had the resources, personnel and institutions needed to meet the bloc's commitments.

In November 2022, ASEAN leaders agreed in principle to admit Timor-Leste and granted it observer status. They later approved a roadmap in May 2023 to help the country meet the requirements for full membership.
Under Gusmão's government, Timor-Leste worked to comply with the requirements across ASEAN's political-security, economic and socio-cultural pillars.
Philippines backs membership bid
The Philippines has supported Timor-Leste's bid to join ASEAN since 2002, with successive administrations maintaining the country's position.
Former president Benigno Aquino III also pledged support for Timor-Leste's membership in 2013.
In May 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. assured then-Timor-Leste Prime Minister Taur Matan Ruak of Manila's support during a meeting on the sidelines of the 42nd ASEAN Summit in Indonesia.
"In the Philippines, you have a partner. We have always been supportive," Marcos said.

Marcos reiterated this during Timorese President José Ramos-Horta's state visit to the Philippines in November 2023. Ramos-Horta said the two countries shared a "long history of solidarity and support for each other."
The Philippines maintained its support even after a diplomatic disagreement with Timor-Leste over the extradition of former Negros Oriental congressman Arnolfo Teves Jr.

In March 2025, a Timorese court rejected the Philippines' request to extradite Teves, who faces multiple murder charges, including over the killing of former governor Roel Degamo. The Philippine government criticized the ruling, saying it went against the trust and cooperation expected among ASEAN members.
In May 2025, the Philippines again expressed support for Timor-Leste's membership ahead of the 46th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur.

Then Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Theresa Lazaro said Manila had committed to supporting Timor-Leste's accession and helping implement the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 following a preparatory meeting on May 24.
The Philippines' renewed assurance came just two months after the disagreement over Teves.
Timor-Leste becomes ASEAN's 11th member

ASEAN leaders agreed to admit Timor-Leste during the bloc's 47th summit in May 2025. The country formally became the 11th member on Oct. 26, 2025, during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
Gusmão signed the declaration on Timor-Leste's admission, while Ramos-Horta attended the ceremony.
Timor-Leste was the first country to join ASEAN since Cambodia in 1999. Its entry also meant the ASEAN emblem, which features rice stalks representing its member states, would have an 11th stalk.
The Manila summit in November 2026 was Timor-Leste's first full ASEAN summit as a member of the regional bloc. — with reports from Cristina Chi, Ian Laqui, Helen Flores and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Marcos: No Pax Silica signing during Trump's ASEAN visit
articles.summary: The Philippines will not sign the Pax Silica agreement during US President Donald Trump's visit for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on…

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 1:02pm

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines will not sign the Pax Silica agreement during US President Donald Trump's visit for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Wednesday, November 18.
The agreement would formalize the country's participation in the US-led initiative to secure global semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains.

Lee Lipton, US ambassador to the Philippines, earlier said that there would be no announcement on the project during the ASEAN Summit this month, but the country's Board of Investments expects the signing to take place before the end of 2026.

Under the agreement, a 4,000-acre industrial center would be built in the Luzon Economic Corridor, beginning with a 1,620-hectare site in New Clark City, Tarlac, which has drawn criticism over alleged environmental degradation and the displacement of farming and fishing communities. The Philippines hub would be the first site developed among members of the Pax Silica consortium.

The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities has described messaging surrounding the initiative as "mixed," saying that important details, such as control over the hub and its products and its environmental impact, remain unclear even as negotiations progress.
Pax Silica is also being oversimplified into an “arms race” between the US and China, organization Executive Director Angelo Kairos dela Cruz said.

Several progressive groups, including renowned Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, have called for the rejection of the project. Protests against Pax Silica have also been held during the summit.

Over 200 individuals were arrested at a protest against the initiative and Trump's visit in Sucat, Muntinlupa, on Sunday, November 15. The 276 protesters, including at least 50 students from the University of the Philippines system, were in police custody for more than two days at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City after a delay in inquest proceedings.
In a report of GMA News, the National Capital Region Police Office said the detainees' transfer to the detention facility was being processed.

articles.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
articles.summary:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to…

blocks.text: The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

blocks.caption: A street scene in Cairo.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
after newsletter promotion
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

blocks.caption: A customer pays for tomatoes with Egyptian pound banknotes at a market in Cairo. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Rubio says US not 'under systemic attack' after series of tech outages
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" supporting theories online that recent disruptions affecting Microsoft, banks and flights are connected.

blocks.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.

Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.
Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.

Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.
Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.
He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.

"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.
Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.
Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages.
"There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC.

"There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."
Beevers said AI is only part of the story.
"It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said.

"Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."

Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."

articles.title: Wages grow at fastest pace since 2023 – but prices are climbing even more quickly
articles.summary:
Wage rates climb about 1 percentage point faster than before pandemic, triggering warnings of a sixth RBA rate rise

Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to…

blocks.text: Wages grew at their fastest pace since late 2023 over the three months to September, buoyed up by this year’s boost to minimum pay rates for millions of lower paid workers – but still not fast enough to keep up with the rising cost of living.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ wage price index climbed by 1.1% in the most recent quarter, lifting the annual increase to 3.5% – a pace that economists said would keep the Reserve Bank on edge about the need for further interest rate hikes.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the pickup in wages growth was thanks to the government’s support for the minimum pay rise.
“We’re helping to deliver higher wages for workers because we know this is one of the best ways to help with the cost of living,” he said.
While wage rates are climbing about 1 percentage point faster per year on average than before the pandemic, prices are climbing even more quickly – a reality that Chalmers recognised.

“Real wages are declining not because wages have been too low but because inflation is still too high, which is why helping in the fight against inflation and getting the budget in better nick are such high priorities for the government.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the latest figures confirmed that “Australians are working harder for less”.
“Australians are poorer under Labor. That is the reality of the economy that has been built by a Labor government that simply does not get it,” he said at a press conference.

items: Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

blocks.text: The Fair Work Commission in early June implemented a 6% pay rise to about 100,000 of the country’s lowest paid employees to help compensate for cost of living pressures made worse by surging fuel prices.
The annual review also gave a 4.75% pay rise to 2.7 million workers on award wages.
Rachael McCririck, head of prices statistics at the ABS, said these decisions “were a key driver of much of the growth in private sector wages this quarter”.
Analysts said wages were growing faster than the Reserve Bank had been expecting, and that this added to the case, if only at the margin, for a potential sixth interest rate hike.

Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said she did not expect a move after the RBA’s final board meeting for the year on 7-8 December, even though the wage growth figure was “uncomfortably high for the central bank”.
“[It’s] unlikely to prompt any immediate reaction, given the economy is now slowing in response to the five interest rate hikes delivered between February and November this year,” Murphy said.
“We expect the central bank will be in wait-and-see mode,” she said.
The ABS figures showed pay rates are rising fastest in the public sector, up by an annual 3.9%, while private sector wages increased by 3.4%.

“The main driver of public sector wage growth was pay rises for state government frontline workers covered by enterprise agreements. This included groups like nurses, midwives and police officers,” McCririck said.
Wages after inflation

Jeff Borland, an economics professor at the University of Melbourne, said while the wage price index was useful to assess inflationary pressures in the labour market, it was less useful as a way to assess workers’ actual incomes.

“The WPI is the labour cost to an employer of having a particular job done. If you want to know what is happening to the average worker, then the weekly income from the [ABS’s] characteristics of employment survey is a better measure,” Borland said.
By this broader measure of worker pay, the story is not as dire as that told by the after-inflation change in the WPI, he said.
Real average hourly labour income received per employed person was artificially boosted through the pandemic but has since come back to be just 3.4% higher this decade.
This extends the overall weak trend through the 2010s, Borland said.
In contrast, the wage price index is down 4.4% since the start of 2020.
“None of the real wage measures are telling you things are going gangbusters,” Borland said.
“But there’s a difference in the degree to which they tell you how badly things are going.”
