articles.summary: Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald.

image.caption: Solace in Winter is a novel by Mary Lawson. ((Penguin Random House Canada, Richard Mobbs))

blocks.text: Books
Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald.
· Hillel Italie
· Posted: Nov 17, 2026 5:28 PM EST | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago

Oprah Winfrey’s new book club pick is an acclaimed Canadian author’s novel about a small community in the late 1960s that’s upended by a young American who has crossed the border to flee the Vietnam War draft.
Solace in Winter, which Winfrey praised as "beautifully written and deeply moving” in a statement, is the November pick for Oprah’s Book Club.
“Solace in Winter reminds us that even in our loneliest moments, unexpected connections can open our hearts, heal old wounds, and change our lives in ways we never imagined,” Winfrey said.

Solace in Winter is a novel set in the small town of Solace in the winter of 1969. It follows a widower named Jack whose quiet life is upended when he finds a dog in a bad way and an injured American draft dodger on the road near his place.
He takes them both in, but when his daughter comes to visit one day, she makes a decision that she can’t take back.

items: 15 Canadian books coming out this November

blocks.text: “I was knocked sideways when Oprah phoned. In fact, to begin with, I didn’t believe it was her. I thought it was a hoax and I nearly hung up. But then she mentioned Solace in Winter, which at that stage hadn’t yet been published, and I thought, just a minute," Lawson told CBC Books in a statement.
"As a writer I am thrilled, of course. As a Canadian, at this particular time, I think it can only be a good thing that a Canadian voice will be heard on the other side of the border. ”

Lawson is also the author of the novels A Town Called Solace, Crow Lake, The Other Side of the Bridge and Road Ends. A Town Called Solace and The Other Side of the Bridge were longlisted for the Booker Prize.
Lawson, currently based in England, is originally from the small farming community of Blackwell, near Sarnia, Ont.

items: Mary Lawson's Booker Prize longlisted novel A Town Called Solace is a mystery about hope and redemption

blocks.text: Oprah's Book Club has been recommending titles since 1996 picked out by Winfrey herself. The book club began as a segment on the The Oprah Winfrey Show.

Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry, selected in November of 2001, and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald, selected in January of 2002.
With files from Cynthia Jimenez

articles.title: FAA halts installation of new routers linked to Friday's airport ground stop until root of problem found
articles.summary: The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travellers, the agency said Tuesday.

image.caption: A JetBlue and American Airlines planes park at gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration lifted a national ground stop issued last Friday. (Eric Lee/Reuters)

blocks.text: World
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration has paused installing routers linked to last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travellers, the agency said Tuesday.
Aviation agency has been struggling to upgrade systems for decades
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has paused installing routers linked to last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travellers, the agency said Tuesday.

The move comes amid growing scrutiny over the nation's air traffic control system and as the Trump administration is making a new request for $50 billion US to improve air travel. Senate Democrats are demanding that the administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.

U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for the nationwide grounding of all planes and upheaval at the nation's airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades, going back well before the first Trump administration.

FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Ark.
Maker of routers says devices were working properly
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA's telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fibre optic lines across the nation.

The ground stop was needed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centres. The centres direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier, also contributed to the trouble.

The FAA said that "excessive data" was flooding the system "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds." That deluge created instability with "aircraft communications and radar feeds," the agency said.

items: U.S. Federal Aviation Administration lifts nationwide ground stop after 4 hours
'Worst is behind us': U.S. officials say air travel recovering from nationwide ground stop

blocks.text: For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday's trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes the routers were working properly when the ground stop occurred. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer," the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
"We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado," he said. "But the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet."
Ground stop aftermath: Why it will take days to get things back to normal
Problems with FAA equipment are decades-old

Upgrading the nation's air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years. Duffy has pushed Congress for billions more dollars, saying just this week much more is needed.
Democrats on the Senate commerce committee said that knowing which device was part of last week's meltdown isn't enough.
"FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues," the Democrats said in a letter sent to Duffy.
The Trump administration on Tuesday sent a letter to key lawmakers outlining its request for $50.1 billion US to modernize the system and make other improvements at airports.

items: United Airlines says issue affecting departing flights has been resolved

blocks.text: The request calls for $10.1 billion US for updating the nation's air traffic control system. Similar amounts would go toward boosting airport infrastructure, replacing or refurbishing terminals at high-impact hubs, constructing five new traffic control centers and improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
"Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster and more efficient," the letter said.
Several Republican senators voiced skepticism following a closed-door meeting Tuesday with the transportation secretary.

A building that housed a router blamed for a technical issue that caused a nationwide ground stop is seen at South Arkansas Regional Airport in El Dorado, Ark. (Penny Chanler/The El Dorado News/The Associated Press)

"I don't think the full $50 billion [US] will be funded. Some of that is not safety-related," said Sen. Ted Cruz, chair of the Senate committee on commerce, science and transportation, which has jurisdiction over air safety issues.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott said he believes the airline industry should pay for the upgrades.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he's open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
Congress approved $12.5 billion US last year for replacing outdated technologies, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction.
Faulty equipment explanation not reassuring, says airline passenger in Toronto delayed by U.S. ground stop
Ground stop cost big airlines over $300M US
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million US combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, analysts said.

The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
"A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend's cancellations did," the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.

articles.title: Federal government waives $4.5B of debt on COVID-19 benefits sent to ineligible recipients
articles.summary: The federal government is writing off billions of dollars' worth of outstanding debt related to COVID-19 benefits sent to individuals it later deemed ineligible.

image.caption: The office of Auditor General Karen Hogan, left, released a report this month saying that billions in debt related to COVID-19 benefits sent to ineligible recipients has been written off. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government is writing off billions of dollars' worth of outstanding debt related to COVID-19 benefits sent to individuals it later deemed ineligible.
Billions in overpaid pandemic-related benefits deemed uncollectable

Last week, the Office of the Auditor General of Canada highlighted that Ottawa had written off approximately $4.5 billion in owed COVID-19 benefits as "uncollectable" during the 2025-26 fiscal year, which ended March 31.
The report noted that's a "significant increase" from $26 million in writeoffs in the previous fiscal year.
Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) told CBC News in a statement that the majority of its pandemic benefit-related writeoffs "pertained to deceased or vulnerable populations."
According to the government's 2026 public accounts report and figures ESDC provided to CBC News, the vast majority of pandemic benefit-related writeoffs took place in the last fiscal year.
Over $5B owed on the books as of July
The Canada Revenue Agency estimates it distributed a total of $14 billion in COVID-19 benefits to individuals it says weren't eligible because they didn't meet the income requirements.
By November 2025, that figure had fallen to about $10 billion, and nearly halved to about $5.56 billion by the end of July.
The agency said in September that the latest debt reduction was due to factors including changes in eligibility and writeoffs.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Ottawa rapidly implemented the Canada emergency response benefit (CERB) under an entirely new piece of legislation. The program remained in place between March and October 2020.

To be eligible for CERB, applicants had to have earned $5,000 in income in the previous 12 months, lost income because of the pandemic and not been receiving employment insurance. The benefit gave recipients $2,000 every four weeks.

items: COVID-19 benefit repayment is hurting low-income Canadians, report says

blocks.text: The CRA has been clear that the Crown retains the right to recover the money it's owed and says it could take legal action against an individual if they have the ability to pay off their debt in full, but allow it to remain unpaid.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
articles.summary:
Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several…

blocks.text: About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.

“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.

Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.

Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.

The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

articles.title: St Kitts and Nevis fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship-by-investment program
articles.summary:
Prime minister of twin-island Caribbean nation announces program wind-down after EU threatens to end visa-free access

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering…

blocks.text: The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.

The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.

In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.

In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.

He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.

“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.

The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy is “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.

“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.

Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

articles.title: 2 hospitalized after CN Rail train derails into Skeena River near Terrace, B.C.
articles.summary: Police say injuries are not life-threatening and cleanup is underway.

image.caption: CN Rail says five of its cars came off the track near Terrace, B.C., on Nov. 17, 2026, falling into the Skeena River. It says no dangerous goods were on board. (Carl J. Reibin)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Updated
Police say injuries are not life-threatening and cleanup is underway.
Injuries are not life-threatening, police say
Two people were taken to hospital after a CN Rail train went off the tracks in northwest B.C. and plunged into the Skeena River.
RCMP say the injuries are non-life-threatening, and cleanup is underway.
Emergency vehicles closed Highway 16 west of Terrace shortly after 1 p.m. PT as police, ambulance and fire crews responded.
It has since been reopened to single-lane alternating traffic.
Multiple emergency vehicles responded to a CN Rail incident west of Terrace, B.C., on Nov. 17, 2026. (Gordon Bonenfant)
Highway 16 is the main artery connecting Terrace to Prince Rupert, where Canada's third-busiest port is used to ship product transported by train and truck to overseas markets.
CN Rail has not said what was on board the train at the time of the derailment, but in a statement said "there are no fires, no dangerous goods and no impact to public safety."
It says one locomotive and five cars derailed. Images from the scene appear to show multiple cars off the track.
Police, ministry of transportation and CN Rail officials remain on the scene.
CN Rail says there were no dangerous goods on the train. (Carl J. Reibin)
With files from Catherine Garrett

articles.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
articles.summary:
Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by…

blocks.text: An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.

The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.

Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

articles.title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
articles.summary: The Metropolitan Police say he has been taken into custody by the US Military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.

blocks.text: A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who has served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC).
Counter Terror Policing said he is now in custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said they had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

articles.title: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers
articles.summary: Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the…

image.caption: Hashim Thaci (pictured here in court in 2023) stepped down as president of Kosovo nearly six years ago to defend himself against war crimes charges Image: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP

blocks.text: A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.
Swift response from government

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.
Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

blocks.caption: The conviction in September of Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders was greeted with shock, disappointment and anger in KosovoImage: Ermal Meta/Matrix Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.
The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."
What is the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.
The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.
For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.
Government set up working group

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

blocks.caption: Speaking of Thaci's September conviction of war crimes in September, Prime Minister Albin Kurti has said that the government of Kosovo 'is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers' Image: Liam McBurney/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."
Parliament considers amending law
In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

blocks.caption: Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute stresses that there is a fundamental difference between criticism of courts based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courtsImage: Bekim Shehu/DW

blocks.text: "Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.
'Room for criticism of both sides'

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

articles.title: Canada's national emergency alert system will sound off Wednesday for testing
articles.summary: Canada's National Public Alerting System is running tests of its Alert Ready system Wednesday across all provinces and territories. Alert Ready delivers alerts about critical events such as…

image.caption: A test of Canada's emergency alert system is set for Wednesday, Nov. 18. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canada's National Public Alerting System is running tests of its Alert Ready system Wednesday across all provinces and territories. Alert Ready delivers alerts about critical events such as tornadoes, flooding, fires and Amber alerts.
Alert Ready test will be broadcast on TV, radio and delivered to wireless devices
There's (probably) no need to take cover if your phone, radio or television blasts out the telltale sounds of an emergency alert Wednesday.

Canada's National Public Alerting System is running tests of its Alert Ready system across all provinces and territories. Alert Ready delivers alerts about critical events such as tornadoes, flooding, fires and Amber alerts.
The test will be broadcast on television and radio and delivered to compatible wireless devices connected to an LTE or 5G network.

items: Ottawa wants us all to have emergency supplies for 3 days. The good news is, that number hasn't changed
New app allows Nova Scotians without cell service to get emergency alerts

blocks.text: "This public test helps ensure the system continues to function effectively and helps Canadians recognize alert signals in the event of a real emergency," Pelmorex, which operates the technical infrastructure of Alert Ready, said in a news release.
The test will simulate an emergency alert, beginning with its distinctive tone, followed by a message that will "clearly indicate that it is a test and that no action is required."
Here's when the tests will happen in each province and territory at local times:
Canadians cannot opt out, Pelmorex noted, "because the system is designed to warn Canadians of imminent threats to life and property."
Tests typically take place in May and November. The CRTC requires wireless service providers and broadcasters to issue at least one public test alert per year, Pelmorex said.
So far in 2026, the system has delivered more than 1,215 emergency alert messages across Canada, notes the news release.

articles.title: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
articles.summary: Russia's defence ministry says it preliminarily believes a technical malfunction was the cause of the crash in the Kemerovo region.

blocks.text: A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.

articles.title: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say
articles.summary:
Bullet hit 72-year-old Fadha Wadha in head outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, in the West Bank, say residents

A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem

blocks.text: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman has been shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in a village near Jericho where settlers have recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the occupied West Bank when she was struck in the head by a bullet as Israeli settlers fired towards Palestinian houses, according to testimonies from residents. Several other Palestinians, including her son, were wounded by gunfire.

Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence had begun when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from its Palestinian residents.

Dozens of Israeli settlers, some of them armed, moved into eight buildings in al-Duyuk al-Tahta two weeks ago with the backing of the settler organisation Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.
“A vehicle carrying settlers chased him,” Younis said. “There were about 15 settlers in several vehicles. They began firing indiscriminately, killing the woman.”
Witnesses said Palestinian residents began to throw stones to defend themselves, as more settlers arrived at the scene, shooting at civilians and injuring six men.

Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was wounded after he rushed to the scene after learning that his mother had been shot. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters he was in shock when he accidentally collided with a parked car belonging to one of the settlers.
Witnesses said the vehicle was empty at the time, but that settlers responded by opening fire, wounding Arafat in the torso.

blocks.caption: Mourners attend the funeral of Wadha Fadha, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman killed by Israeli settlers, near Jericho. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Naama Fidhat said her husband was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah when Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him. She said Israeli soldiers also arrested their son, Wadha’s grandson, early the following morning.
“What did we do? We didn’t do anything,” she said. “This is our house, they were the ones who came with weapons … we were unarmed, we were sleeping.”

The Israeli military said a group of Palestinians in ​a car “accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it”. It said the Palestinians exited the vehicle and attacked the Israelis, who opened fire at the Palestinians. “There are Israeli and Palestinian ​casualties in the incident,” the military said.
The arrival of the Israeli settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta had raised fears among Palestinian residents who have faced repeated attacks in the area.

The Binyamin regional council, which covers 47 illegal settlements, claimed the properties in the village had been bought from Palestinians, but Jericho’s governor, Hussein Hamayel, disputed the claim, saying the land belonged to the state and could not legally be sold.
Human rights activists said settlers had assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg during the takeover earlier this month.

“Since the settlers moved into the area on 4 November our lives have been turned upside down,” Younis told the Guardian. “We used to live peacefully and safely on our farms, but since the settlers arrived, our lives have become a living hell. I own 53 dunams [5.3 hectares] of farmland with greenhouses, but we are no longer allowed to access them. We have suffered devastating financial losses, and now people are being killed as well.”

There has been a sharp ​rise in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the West Bank, territory Israel captured in the 1967 six-day war. UN bodies and most ​countries deem the settlements illegal, which Israel disputes.

On Tuesday, Suleiman Abu Srour, a photographer for the Palestinian news agency Wafa, was beaten by Israeli soldiers while covering events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta. Wafa said he suffered fractures and bruises, was detained for six hours and had his phone confiscated before being released.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

articles.title: ‘Godmother’ of illegal Israeli West Bank settler project Daniella Weiss among group sanctioned by Australia
articles.summary:
Foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank.
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
‘Godmother’ of settler movement

Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers.
She and Nachala have also advocated for the settlement of Israelis in Gaza and the expulsion of Palestinians from the area.

The 80-year-old was previously the mayor of Kedumim, an Israeli settlement in the West Bank where far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has also been sanctioned by the Australian government, also lives.

blocks.caption: Nachala movement leader Daniella Weiss is known as the ‘godmother’ of the settler movement. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images

blocks.text: Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.

Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
The government said the sanctions were coordinated with the UK, who announced sanctions on Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the “status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable”.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza.”
More settlements had been approved under the four years of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government than in the previous 20 years.
Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot, has said that he would take a tougher approach than Netanyahu on settler violence.

blocks.caption: The E1 corridor in the occupied West Bank, where Israel is planning more settlements.  Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Australia expecting backlash
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night, and outlined Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
after newsletter promotion
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Recent analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo showed 85 of 132 food shipments over eight years had contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australian sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had done in the past.

“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the [now] caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
‘Brazen breach of law’
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said the sanctions did not go far enough to stop illegal settlements or take action against the Israeli government.
The minor party has pushed the government to join other nations including the UK and Canada to ban imports of products made in illegal settlements.
“This announcement won’t touch most of the hundreds of businesses that have a role in this brazen breach of international law, or the Israeli government that backs them,” Shoebridge said.
The government warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network president, Nasser Mashni, pushed for further sanctions against individuals, companies and the Israeli government.
“Australia has sanctioned a company that builds illegal settlements. Now sanction the Israeli government that orders Palestinian homes demolished,” he said.

articles.title: Calgary high school says too many students are getting food delivered
articles.summary: A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.

image.caption: St. Francis High School sent parents a memo Monday outlining concerns about the "increased use of food delivery apps" by students. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.
St. Francis asks parents to ask kids to stop ordering food during class time

In the letter, St. Francis High School administrators said while the deliveries may be convenient, they can also be disruptive to classrooms, and pose security risks to have students interacting with individuals they don’t know on school grounds.

“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day," the letter said.

Lee Martin, who represents Calgary Catholic teachers for the Alberta Teachers’ Association, told CBC News it's become more of an issue in recent years. He heard from one teacher just this week who said a driver tried to deliver food right to a classroom window.
“I think that as public educators we want our children fed,” said Martin. “However, this seems to be a bit out of control.”
A food drop-off cart outside an elementary school in Calgary's southeast. (Submitted by Lee Martin)
And it’s not only at high schools.

At one elementary school, he said upwards of 30 parents were either dropping off food or sending deliveries there daily, so the school set up a table in the foyer where students can go search for their bag at lunchtime.
A spokesperson for the Calgary Catholic School District said to their knowledge, St. Francis is the only school in its board addressing the matter.
In a statement, the Calgary Board of Education said it doesn’t have a specific policy on food deliveries, and it’s up to principals at individual schools to set guidelines if it is an issue.
“Students are discouraged from ordering deliveries into the building, though we are aware they may meet the driver in other locations on school property,” the statement said.
Students say it’s common, not necessarily an issue
Outside St. Francis, delivery driver Ali Nuru dropped off food for a student Tuesday. He says he’ll typically end up doing a couple of school deliveries a week.
“Most of the time I bring from McDonald's,” he said.
Delivery driver Ali Nuru says he typically delivers a couple of times a week to high schools, with McDonald's the No. 1 meal of choice. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)
Students said it’s fairly routine to see classmates meeting drivers in the parking lot to pick up their orders.

“A lot of times — I'm kind of snitching — but they'll be like, ‘oh can I go to the bathroom' and then they just go meet the driver around the school, like the front of the school and then bring the food in with them,” said Grade 11 student Rebira Assefa.
However, she said it hasn’t been a big deal in her classrooms, with most students unbothered by it.
The bathroom excuse can be an issue though, said Grade 11 student Bradley White, since only so many students are allowed out of a class at a time.
“Like if someone's out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one's allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” said White.
Plus, he said it can be a distraction when someone orders an “excessive” amount of food for themselves and their friends, and brings it into class.
Cracking down on it, though, could be tricky.

“I don't really know how they would enforce a policy where you're not allowed to order something, because kids are going to do it anyways. They'll end up rebelling because you put another policy in,” said Grade 12 student Alysa Utigard.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca
With files from Colleen Underwood

articles.title: Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
articles.summary: A cache of internal records outlines the bank's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump and Russian oligarchs. The German lender has sought to deflect criticism by claiming its bad behavior is a…

image.caption: Dark days ahead for Germany's biggest lender? Deutsche Bank shares plunged on Tuesday after the publication of damning internal documentsImage: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP

blocks.text: Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."

The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.

Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.

Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.
Money laundering, oligarchs, terrorists: How corrupt are the banks?
Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians

In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.

Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways?

Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.

When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.
Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership.

"When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so."
The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.
German government wants 'full transparency' from Deutsche Bank
Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.

In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."
A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.

Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."
Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.
'Still easy to avoid regulatory checks'

articles.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
articles.summary: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.

blocks.text: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

articles.title: Who to watch in Spain's election race
articles.summary: Spain votes on 29 November, with the conservatives and the far right favourites to win after eight years of Socialist-led rule.

blocks.text: Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.
He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.
Sánchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.
The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.
He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.

José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.
In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".
Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.

Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.

Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.
He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".
The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.

His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.

He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.
Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.
Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.

Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.
Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.

Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.

Socialist Carlos Cuerpo, 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.

He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".
In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."

Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

articles.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
articles.summary:
High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional…

blocks.text: Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce, under Secretary Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by Attorney General Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.
